claims.feature: reading standard: account for every detail
claims.claim: The critic's test for a Wolfe reading is a consistent account of why everything in the text is there, in a story of under 3,000 words.
claims.quote: why everything that's in the text is there

claims.claim: Names are always important in Wolfe stories; Stromboli evokes Pinocchio and the planet Sarg the marionettist Tony Sarg.
claims.quote: Names are always important in Wolfe stories.

claims.claim: Central plot points are skipped over and referred to only in retrospect, others presented misdirectingly, others never cleared up.
claims.quote: Central plot points are skipped over

claims.feature: liar plus translator frame leaves motive underdetermined
claims.claim: Because Severian is known to lie and Wolfe poses as translator of a manuscript for an unknown audience, the text's purpose and the narrator's motives are underdetermined.
claims.quote: underdetermined with regard to Severian's motives

claims.feature: archaic Latinate words that look like neologisms
claims.claim: The style uses words that appear to be neologisms but are archaic, often Latin-derived usages, evoking strangeness while preserving meaning.
claims.quote: words that appear to be neologisms but are anything but

claims.claim: Auerbach reports Clute's argument that the whole narrative is a put-on to justify Severian's taking power.
claims.quote: a put-on to justify Severian taking power

claims.claim: After The Book of the New Sun Wolfe abandoned baroque long sentences and strove for a more minimalistic surface text.
claims.quote: abandons the baroque and long sentences

claims.feature: subtext replaces text in late work
claims.claim: In the post-Wizard Knight novels the subtext tends to replace the text, and Wolfe plays less fair by withholding metatextual repetitions.
claims.quote: The subtext tends to replace the text.

claims.claim: Aramini's reading principle: something is true about almost every detail, literally or figuratively, so he reads without suspicion and makes everything true somehow.
claims.quote: everything has to be true somehow, literally or figuratively

claims.feature: two mysteries that explain each other
claims.claim: Wolfe sometimes plants two confusing things that explain each other, as with the context-free gunfight and the off-screen death in Home Fires.
claims.quote: the two mysteries explain each other

claims.feature: literalized metaphor and repeated unrelated fact
claims.claim: Wolfe controls meaning through logic, small details, literalized metaphors and juxtaposing unrelated things; tunnel dogs called gods signal that gods are stored in the tunnels.
Embedded tales map allegorically onto the larger story, and symbols are built to yield concrete plot conclusions.
claims.quote: embeds tales which map allegorically to the larger story

claims.claim: Wolfe told Nigel Price that, having so often been called a difficult writer, he strove in later works to make his style simpler and more accessible.
claims.source: Aramini interview, Ultan's Library 2020 (Price reporting Wolfe)
claims.quote: make his style simpler and more accessible

claims.feature: classic detective stories as stylistic model
claims.claim: Price suggests Wolfe's late reading of Rex Stout and Sayers supplied the stylistic model for his late books, e.g. Wizard Knight as heroic fantasy channelling Stout.
claims.quote: they provided the stylistic model for his writing

claims.feature: elided structures point to one solution
claims.claim: Aramini holds Wolfe is a modernist who merely pretends to inconclusive subjectivity; his elided structures point at implied correct conclusions.
claims.quote: merely pretends to create inconclusive subjectivity

verdicts.trueWording: "a reading that gives a consistent account of why everything that's in the text is there"; "a story of, I guess, no more than 3000 words"
verdicts.note: Raw page fetched live (HTTP 200, curl + browser UA). Quote appears word for word in Graham Sleight's Locus Roundtable post on 'The Toy Theater'. Both limbs supported: the reading standard and the under-3,000-word length ('no more than 3000 words').

verdicts.trueWording: "Names are always important in Wolfe stories"; Stromboli = Disney's Pinocchio; "Sarg, after the famous marionettist Tony Sarg"
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim in the post body. Stromboli limb verbatim in the body ('meant to remind us of the monstrous puppet-buyer in Disney's Pinocchio (1940)'). Sarg limb is in the comment thread, which the source field explicitly includes ('with comments'): 'Another significant, if rather obvious, name is that of the planet, Sarg, after the famous marionettist Tony Sarg.'

verdicts.trueWording: "Central plot points are skipped over and only referred to in retrospect. Others are presented in a highly misdirecting manner. And others are simply never cleared up."
verdicts.note: Raw page fetched live (HTTP 200). Quote verbatim; all three limbs (elision-then-retrospect, misdirection, never resolved) present consecutively in the same paragraph.

verdicts.trueWording: "These two facts cause the book to be underdetermined with regard to Severian's motives and to the purpose of the text itself."
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim. Every limb supported in the same paragraph: 'We know that Severian is a liar quite early on', 'Wolfe claims to be acting as a translator of Severian's manuscript', 'without knowing anything about that audience'.

verdicts.trueWording: "words that appear to be neologisms but are anything but, drawn... from archaic words and usages, often Latin-derived"
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim. Purpose limb also verbatim on the page: 'to evoke strangeness while preserving a depth of meaning'.

verdicts.trueWording: "John Clute argued that the whole thing is a put-on to justify Severian taking power."
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim in the comment thread, posted by 'Mr. Waggish' — the blog's own author, David Auerbach (masthead: 'David Auerbach on literature, tech, film, etc.'; post byline 'David Auerbach'). Reporting-attribution limb therefore holds. Page field 'comments' is accurate.

verdicts.trueWording: "after the publication of The Book of the New Sun, when he abandons the baroque and long sentences and often strives for a more minimalistic surface text"
verdicts.note: Raw page fetched live (HTTP 200). Quote verbatim in Aramini's answer ('Marc:' block). Both limbs — post-New Sun timing and the minimalistic surface text — in the same sentence.

verdicts.trueWording: "his post Wizard Knight novels... The subtext tends to replace the text."; "he doesn't provide as many metatextual repetitions... I feel he started to play less and less fair"
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim, and immediately preceded on the page by 'how utterly difficult getting to the bottom of his post Wizard Knight novels can be', supporting the post-Wizard Knight limb. The play-less-fair limb is supported later in the same interview (Aramini on 'his late work'), phrased as late work rather than post-Wizard Knight specifically, which the interview treats as the same body of books.

verdicts.trueWording: "everything has to be true somehow, literally or figuratively, so I do not read with suspicion"; "make everything true SOMEHOW"
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim in an Aramini ('Marc:') answer. The 'almost every detail' limb is separately verbatim earlier in the same interview: 'something is true about almost every detail which is included in the text.'

verdicts.trueWording: "until we realize that the two mysteries explain each other"; "a gunfight that is entirely removed from all context"; "killed off-screen"
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim. Home Fires, the context-free gunfight and the off-screen death of the investigator are all named in the same paragraph; the generalisation limb is stated just above it: 'Sometimes Wolfe employs two confusing or mysterious things in a text that will explain each other.'

verdicts.trueWording: "Logic, small details, the literalization of metaphors, and the juxtaposition of two seemingly unrelated things... are all means through which Wolfe controls his narrative"
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim. Tunnel-dogs limb verbatim earlier: 'the dogs running rampant in the tunnels are called gods. There are gods in the tunnels... many of the gods of the Whorl are actually stored in the tunnels, as repeating an unrelated fact in the text will objectively state.'

verdicts.trueWording: "He uses sophisticated techniques such as the mise en abyme, embeds tales which map allegorically to the larger story... creates symbols and metaphors to produce concrete plot conclusions."
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim. Both limbs (allegorical mapping of embedded tales; symbols engineered to yield concrete plot conclusions) sit in the same sentence.

verdicts.trueWording: "Wolfe told me once that, having been told so often that he was considered 'a difficult writer,' he strove in his later works to make his style simpler and more accessible."
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim, spoken in a 'Nigel:' turn. Interviewer identified on the page as 'Ultan's Library co-editor Nigel Price', so the 'told Nigel Price' limb holds.

verdicts.trueWording: "for pleasure he was mostly reading classic detective stories, and I think that they provided the stylistic model for his writing"
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim in Nigel Price's turn. Stout/Sayers limb verbatim: 'He loved the Nero Wolfe mysteries and the Lord Peter Winsey stories of Dorothy L. Sayers'. Wizard Knight limb verbatim: 'The Wizard Knight is Wolfe writing heroic fantasy as if he were channeling Rex Stout.' The page says the model was for 'his writing' rather than literally 'his late books', but the sentence is scoped by 'In terms of his own reading at this time' within an exchange about Wolfe's late works, so the limb is supported.

verdicts.trueWording: "Wolfe is a modernist who merely pretends to create inconclusive subjectivity; his elided structures point at 'correct' conclusions that are often implied."
verdicts.note: Raw page fetched live (HTTP 200) — the 2013 Ultan's Library interview 'Shadows of the New Sun: Marc Aramini'. Quote verbatim; both limbs (feigned inconclusive subjectivity, elided structures pointing at implied correct conclusions) in one sentence spoken by Aramini.
